title: Pesticide misuse among small Andean farmers stems from pervasive misinformation by retailers
screen_reason: Mystery-shopper audit in which incognito farmers presented a fictional pest problem to 1,489 pesticide retailers across the Bolivian, Ecuadorian and Peruvian highlands and recorded the advice given; the recommendations were then checked against manufacturers' product datasheets. 88.2% were incorrect (only 11.8% correct end to end). That is a share of items in a sample judged inaccurate against an external documentary standard, i.e. CONTENT under the governing denominator rule, and the review's definition of misinformation explicitly extends to 'inaccurate or misleading (health) content'. Flagged borderline=true: the medium is face-to-face commercial advice rather than media content, the errors are dosing and product-adequacy errors rather than false claims about the world, and the paper's own framing of 'misinformation' is looser than the review's. If the review restricts CONTENT to mediated information this is the paper to drop, and the borderline flag plus this note make that a one-step decision.

estimates.platform: In-person pesticide retail outlets (shops, chain stores, market and itinerant retailers, distributors, wholesalers)
estimates.date: Not reported. Collection necessarily predates the 14 June 2021 submission; the paper was published 21 June 2022
estimates.measure_type: % of pesticide retailers' recommendations that failed to follow the manufacturer's datasheet standards (wrong pest identification, wrong product type, product not licensed for the crop-pest pair, or dose outside the label bounds)
estimates.value_raw: 88.2% of recommendations incorrectly followed standards; equivalently 'only 11.8% of retailer's recommendations were correct throughout the entire recommendation process'
estimates.denominator: Recommendations elicited in 1,489 incognito surveys of pesticide retailers across 46 Andean localities in 15 regions of Bolivia, Ecuador and Peru; the surveys yielded 9,670 individual product recommendations, which were aggregated to one verdict per survey ('when retailers recommended several products, these recommendations were considered as correct only if all the products were adequate for the pest and all their doses were correct'). Cases classifiable as neither right nor wrong were dropped, so the effective denominator is somewhat under 1,489 and is never printed.
estimates.definition: A recommendation counted as correct only if it passed all four sequential checks against the product datasheet: the pest species was correctly identified (broad terms such as 'larva' or 'insect' counted as incorrect); the product type matched the pest phylum (insecticide for insects, fungicide for fungi); the product's datasheet listed both the crop and the pest; and the recommended dose, converted from local units such as spoons and bottle caps, fell within the datasheet's lower and upper bounds. Anything else counted in the 88.2%.
estimates.misinfo_def: The paper offers no definition of misinformation; the title and framing treat inaccurate retailer advice as such, and the operational criterion is discordance with 'official recommendations provided by manufacturers': "an empirical study was co-constructed and conducted by a network of local farmers in the Andes to assess the overall quality of recommendations by pesticide retailers compared to official recommendations provided by manufacturers"
estimates.n: 1,489 retailer surveys (9,670 individual product recommendations), less an unstated number of unclassifiable cases
estimates.source_quote: the results suggest that 88.2% of recommendations standards were incorrectly
estimates.page_loc: Abstract, p. 1, and Results Section 3.1 'Errors in retailer recommendations', p. 6, with Fig 1 (accumulation of errors along the recommendation process)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Researcher comparison against documentary reference standards, not human judgement of plausibility: pest names harmonised in OpenRefine against an expert-built synonymy table; commercial product names matched to national pesticide databases; active substances reconciled via Wikidata; modes of action classified with IRAC v9.4 and FRAC; doses converted with an expert-built local-to-international unit table and compared with datasheet bounds. This is a strong, auditable ground truth (data are open at Zenodo, doi 10.5281/zenodo.5813509) but it is a regulatory-label standard, not a truth/falsity adjudication, and no inter-coder reliability is reported for the harmonisation steps or for the incognito farmers' recall of what the retailer said.
estimates.moderator_quote: Surveys were carried out by incognito farmers to obtain responses reflecting the realities experienced by local farmers asking for pesticide recommendations. Incognito farmers were local ones or students in agronomy who came to the retailer with a fictional pest problem asking for retailer's help. ... Within these localities, an exhaustive sampling was performed with a two-step process. First, official lists of retailers available from the ministries of agriculture were used to plan the survey's route. Second, if additional retailers were accidentally encountered on the route, they were also surveyed.
estimates.notes: Design strengths worth carrying into any synthesis: the retailers did not know they were being studied (no Hawthorne effect, no consent - an explicit ethical trade-off the authors defend), retailers within the chosen localities were enumerated exhaustively from ministry registries plus opportunistic additions, and the standard is documentary rather than judgemental. Confidence is held at medium for three reasons: (a) the exact denominator behind 88.2% is never printed, because Fig 1's 'unknown' category was 'excluded from the calculation of proportions' at each of four dependent steps, so the true n sits somewhere below 1,489; (b) recommendations were reconstructed from the incognito shopper's memory immediately after the visit, not recorded, so the input is recalled speech; (c) no data-collection date is given anywhere, so year falls back to publication (2022) per the protocol, though collection must predate the 14 June 2021 submission - treat the year as soft. denom_selection=curated because the stimulus was a designed set of 11 crops and 20 expert-chosen pest complexes rather than whatever farmers happened to ask about; topic=other because the subject matter is agronomic advice, with health consequences but no health claim. population_scope=professional: the producers of the content are commercial retailers, not the general public. breadth=false rather than misleading because each verdict is a binary match/mismatch against a documented bound, not a judgement of spin. The abstract sits alongside a journal sidebar in the extracted text, so the source_quote is trimmed to the contiguous span carrying the value; the full sentence is in rob.item10_quote.

missed_or_uncertain: The step-level error rates in Fig 1 and Section 3.1 were deliberately not extracted as separate rows: 23.3% of retailers misidentified the pest species, 13.9% proposed the wrong product type, 48.7% proposed an erroneous pesticide for the pest, 52.4% recommended an inadequate dose. Fig 1's caption is explicit that 'each step is dependent on the previous steps', so each of these sits on a different, unprinted conditional denominator (the subset that survived the earlier steps); they are not independent estimates and cannot be combined, and any of them presented as a standalone prevalence share would misstate its base. The same applies to Fig 2's dosage split (47.9% proper dose, 33.5% overdose up to 8x the upper bound, 18.6% underdose down to a fifth of the proper dose) - a three-way partition of the dose-assessable subset only, whose size is not given; note also that this 47.9% 'proper dose' is not the complement of the 52.4% inadequate-dose figure on the same base, which is a further reason to leave the step level alone. Also not extracted: (1) 79.2% of recommended products pertaining to only 6 modes of action, 25.4% of mixtures combining products with the same mode of action, 13.8% mixing insecticide with fungicide, 19.5% including a multi-active-ingredient product, 23.2%/8.8% of recommendations carrying two/three-plus products - these describe resistance risk and product composition, not accuracy. (2) '93.4% of correct recommendations occurred for pests and diseases of potato' - a within-correct-class composition. (3) The expert-model results on replacing highly toxic products - a counterfactual simulation. (4) Toxicity classifications (WHO categories, EU non-approved substances) - hazard, not accuracy. The one open uncertainty I could not resolve from the text: whether the 88.2% denominator is the 1,489 surveys or some subset, and how the 9,670 individual product recommendations map onto it. The Methods state the aggregation rule (all products must be adequate and correctly dosed) which implies a survey-level denominator, and the Results interchange 'retailers' and 'recommendations' when quoting step-level percentages, which supports that reading; but the abstract's headline count of 9,670 leaves room for a product-level denominator, which would change n by a factor of six without changing the percentage.

rob.design: Cross-sectional covert audit ('mystery shopper') study, co-designed with a farmer network. Sampling: 46 smallholder localities across 15 regions of Bolivia, Ecuador and Peru, purposively chosen for varying pesticide intensity and crop mix; within each locality retailers were enumerated exhaustively from ministry-of-agriculture registries, with additional shops added opportunistically along the route, giving 1,489 retailers of every type (shops, chain stores, market, itinerant, distributors, wholesalers) and 9,670 recommendations. Instrument: a local farmer or agronomy student presented a co-designed, realistic fictional pest story plus a locally taken photograph of the pest, and asked for identification, product names, dose and frequency, plus organic alternatives; nothing was bought; researchers debriefed the shopper immediately afterwards into KoBoToolbox. Retailers were not consented, deliberately, to avoid a Hawthorne effect; anonymity was preserved and visits were made only when no customers were present. Assessment: four dependent checks against manufacturer datasheets and national pesticide databases, with unclassifiable cases excluded from the proportions. Data and code open (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.5813509). Weaknesses for this review: no data-collection dates; no reliability statistics for the shopper's recall or for the name-harmonisation steps; the denominator behind the headline figure is not printed; unmatched commercial names and unspecified concentrations were dropped from the product and dosage assessments respectively, which is a non-random exclusion likely to remove the least documentable (and plausibly least standard) recommendations. Funder (McKnight Foundation) 'helped with study design' but had no role in collection, analysis or publication.
rob.item6_quote: Adequacy between retailer's recommendation and recommended use from datasheets was assessed in a three-step manner. First, the broad adequacy between pest phylum (insects or fungi) and product type (insecticide or fungicide) was assessed. Second, the presence of pest name (either Spanish or scientific name) and crop on the products' datasheets was checked for. A product was considered adequate if both the pest and the crop were present on its datasheet and inadequate if either crop or pest species were missing. ... Then, converted dosages were classified as correct if they fell within the lower and upper bounds from datasheets, as overuse if higher than the upper bound, and as underuse if lower than the lower bound.
rob.item10_quote: An empirical study was conducted with smallholder farmers who collected 9,670 pesticide retailers' recommendations from 1489 surveys in the highlands of Bolivia, Ecuador and Peru. ... the results suggest that 88.2% of recommendations standards were incorrectly followed resulting in dosing recommendations that were either excessive or insufficient and accurate less than 12% of the time.
